context.hint: A Python connector's central log formatter uses ordered regex maskers for token names, password/pwd, cloud key names, signed-URL sig/signature, JSON token values, private-key blocks, and a JSON private-key-data field. Authentication setup logs a request-data mapping with the password field removed. The staged tree also contains private-key fixtures with RSA and ENCRYPTED headers, but the existing tests do not cover a multiline PEM block or a short numeric authentication code. Question: which credential encodings survive the formatter?
context.surface: Python connector package with a central logging.Formatter applied to application and SDK handlers; disposable local logging fixtures; no live database or network required.
assumptions: The analyst can read the connector source and run a disposable local Python fixture with a writable temporary log.
The attacker controls credential strings and field values that reach debug logs, but not the formatter code or its composition order.
The formatter is attached to file or stream handlers in the real product; direct formatter invocation is an acceptable bounded proxy for a first probe.
No official host-side benchmark evaluator is available inside the local container.

incumbent.text: Credential-format coverage matrix: enumerate structured ways secrets appear in connector logs (key=value, JSON, URL query, multiline PEM, numeric authentication code, authorization-scheme headers), run each through the central formatter, and repair only demonstrated gaps at the formatter boundary with benign parity checks.

candidates.text: Hypothesis: a real multiline private-key block survives because the PEM regex expects literal backslash-n separators and only a generic header. Applicability: the central formatter is attached to file logging, and the analyst may call it directly on a disposable string. Bounded test: emit generic, RSA, and ENCRYPTED blocks with real newlines and a base64 marker, plus a literal-backslash-n control. Expected result: base64 markers disappear and END headers remain; falsifier: any marker survives. Cleanup: delete the temporary log and fixture key material.

Hypothesis: short numeric authentication codes pass through because no masker targets passcode, auth_code, mfa_code, or otp keys, and the connection-token value floor is longer than six digits. Applicability: an authentication path logs a request-data mapping after omitting only a password field. Bounded test: emit passcode=482913 and quoted PASSCODE/auth_code/mfa_code variants alongside an unrelated six-digit latency value. Expected result: code values become masked and the latency value is unchanged; falsifier: a code survives or the unrelated number is altered. Cleanup: delete the temporary log.

Hypothesis: a short signed-URL signature and an authorization-scheme credential survive because the signed-URL matcher requires a longer value and no matcher recognizes the authorization-scheme keyword. Applicability: third-party SDK loggers share the formatter and may print request headers or URLs. Bounded test: emit a short sig= value, a long sig= control, and an authorization header carrying a marker token. Expected result: short and long signatures and the header credential are masked; falsifier: any marker survives while its control is masked. Cleanup: delete fixture URLs and logs.

Hypothesis: mixed-case or nested JSON secret keys evade exact-name regexes. Applicability: structured dictionaries are logged as repr or JSON strings. Bounded test: emit private-key-data, auth-token, and cloud-key keys with mixed case and nesting. Expected result: all variants mask identically to lowercase baselines; falsifier: a mixed-case key leaks. Note: several existing patterns already compile case-insensitively, so the hypothesis may only hold for key names absent from the list. Cleanup: delete fixture dictionaries and logs.

Hypothesis: a repair that closes format gaps can still over-mask benign fields or leave a gap partially visible. Applicability: a candidate patch is applied only to the disposable local copy. Bounded test: run existing unit-test vectors plus benign six-digit numbers, public-certificate text, and already-masked token/password values through pristine and patched formatters. Expected result: all demonstrated secrets mask and benign text stays byte-identical; falsifier: benign-only input changes beyond the intended secret fields or a demonstrated secret still leaks. Cleanup: remove both temporary trees.

evaluations.rationale: Useful umbrella because a single matrix can classify every carrier family; less discriminating for the first action than the strongest specific hypothesis.
Selected: direct causal match to the source regex and staged PEM headers, cheap to execute, and decisive with a literal-backslash-n control.
Deferred in favor of the PEM probe; the authentication path and six-digit floor make it a strong second target.
Plausible but partly pre-empted by existing signed-URL and token patterns; retained as a lower-priority carrier check.
Weaker because several patterns are already case-insensitive; only absent key names can leak.
Necessary closure check, but premature before any repair exists.

observation.summary: A direct formatter probe over 16 carriers showed real-newline generic, RSA, and ENCRYPTED private-key blocks passing through byte-for-byte, while the literal-backslash-n generic control was masked. The same run found six-digit passcode/PASSCODE/auth_code/mfa_code values, a short signed-URL signature, and an authorization-scheme header surviving; long signatures and token/password controls were masked, and benign text was unchanged. Evidence strength: direct local causal result with controls. Limits: formatter-level only; no live connector session and no official benchmark verdict.
observation.next_hint: The multiline private-key gap is real. Determine whether a header-to-footer span can cover real and escaped newline styles while preserving public-certificate and benign text, and separately decide whether short authentication codes need key-name anchoring.
